en: Thus have I heard— Dīgha Nikāya 3: The Ambaṭṭha Sutta.

On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Icchānaṅgala.
There, the Blessed One stayed in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove.
1. The Account of Pokkharasāti

Now at that time, the brahmin Pokkharasāti was residing in Ukkaṭṭhā—a place populous with beings, abundant in grass, timber, water, and grain, a royal domain granted as a royal gift and a brahminical endowment by King Pasenadi of Kosala.
The brahmin Pokkharasāti heard:
"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is wandering on tour among the Kosalans."
Together with a large community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks,
he arrived at Icchānaṅgala and was staying at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove.
Now, this excellent report of the venerable Gotama’s fame has spread abroad:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
2. Ambaṭṭha the Young Man
Now at that time, the brahmin Pokkharasāti had a young brahmin student named Ambaṭṭha,
who was a reciter, a master of the mantras, one who had gone to the further shore of the three Vedas— including the Nighaṇḍus and the Keṭubhas,
along with phonology and etymology, and history as the fifth— as well as a grammarian and an expert in cosmology and the marks of a Great Man, being authorized and acknowledged [as such].
In the ancient tradition of the teachers learned in the three Vedas, it was said:
"What I know, you know; what you know, I know."
Then the brahmin Pokkharasāti addressed the young man Ambaṭṭha:
"Dear Ambaṭṭha, this ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan,
is wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a great saṅgha of monks, about five hundred monks in number, and has arrived at Icchānaṅgala."
He has arrived and is staying at Icchānaṅgala, in the grove of Icchānaṅgala.
Regarding that venerable Gotama, a beautiful report of his fame has spread abroad:

"Truly, that Blessed One is an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
Thus, having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life (brahmacariya), which is entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.”
"Come, dear Ambaṭṭha, go to where the ascetic Gotama is; having approached him, find out whether the reputation that has arisen concerning the venerable Gotama is true or not.
Whether the venerable Gotama is such as he is reported to be or not, we shall know the venerable Gotama for what he truly is.
"But how, sir, shall I find out about the venerable Gotama: 'Whether the venerable..."
“Whether the report that has arisen concerning Gotama is true or not, whether that venerable Gotama is such as he is said to be or not?
“My dear Ambaṭṭha, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man have come down to us in our mantras; for a Great Man endowed with these, there are only two possible destinies and no other.”

If he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of righteousness, conqueror of the four quarters, stabilizer of the land, and possessor of the seven treasures.
These are his seven treasures:
namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, he has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean without punishment or sword, but through righteousness, he dwells therein.
But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, who draws back the veil from the world.
"But I, dear Ambaṭṭha, am the giver of the mantras;
you are the receiver of the mantras.
"Very well, sir," the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha replied to the brahmin Pokkharasāti, and having assented, he rose from his seat.
Having paid homage to the brahmin Pokkharasāti and circumambulated him,
he mounted a chariot drawn by mares and set out for the forest grove of Icchānaṅgala together with a large number of young brahmins.
Traveling by carriage as far as the ground would allow, he alighted from the carriage and entered the monastery on foot.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were walking back and forth in the open air.
Then the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha approached those bhikkhus; having approached them, he said this to those bhikkhus:
“Where, sirs, does that venerable Gotama dwell at present?”
“For it is to see that venerable Gotama that we have come here.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“This young man Ambaṭṭha is of a well-known clan and is a pupil of the renowned brahmin Pokkharasāti.”
"Indeed, the Blessed One engages in such conversation with young men of good family.
They said this to the young man Ambaṭṭha:
"Ambaṭṭha, this dwelling has its door closed. Approach it quietly and without haste; having entered the porch, cough and knock on the bolt. The Blessed One will open the door for you."

Then the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha approached that dwelling with its door closed; approaching quietly and unhurriedly, he entered the porch, coughed, and knocked on the bolt. The Blessed One opened the door. The young brahmin Ambaṭṭha entered.
The young brahmins also entered and exchanged greetings with the Blessed One; having concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side.
But the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, while walking, exchanged various polite greetings with the seated Blessed One; while standing, he also exchanged various polite greetings with the seated Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One said this to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha:
“Is it indeed thus, Ambaṭṭha, that you [behave] with the elder, aged brahmins, the seniors, and the teachers of teachers?”
“Is there conversation between us, such that while I am walking or standing, you, sitting down, exchange some appropriate words with me?
“No indeed, Master Gotama. 2.1. First Boast of Superiority:
“This is not so, Master Gotama.”
For indeed, Master Gotama, a brahmin walking is worthy of conversing with a brahmin walking;
a brahmin standing is worthy of conversing with a brahmin standing;
a brahmin sitting is worthy of conversing with a brahmin sitting; [and a brahmin] lying down...
"For indeed, Master Gotama, a Brahmin deserves to converse with a Brahmin who is lying down.
But even with those shavelings, these wretched ascetics, these outcasts, the dark offspring of our kinsmen, my conversation is just as it is with you, Master Gotama.
"But, Ambaṭṭha, your coming here was not without purpose. Whatever purpose you had for coming, you should pay close attention to that very purpose."
“Indeed, sir, this young man Ambaṭṭha has lived the life; he is one who fancies himself as having lived it—what else could it be but because he has not actually lived it?

Then, being addressed by the Blessed One with the words “one who has not lived the life,” the young man Ambaṭṭha became angry and displeased. Slandering the Blessed One, disparaging the Blessed One, and reviling the Blessed One, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama will be made to look even worse than I,” he said this to the Blessed One:
“The Sakyan clan, Master Gotama, is fierce;
the Sakyan clan, Master Gotama, is harsh;
the Sakyan clan, Master Gotama, is fickle.”
"The Sakyans, Master Gotama, are of the clan of the Ibbhas;
being of the clan of the Ibbhas, they do not honor brahmins, they do not revere brahmins, they do not esteem brahmins, they do not worship brahmins, and they do not pay homage to brahmins.
This, Master Gotama, is not fitting, this is not appropriate, that these Sakyans, being of the clan of the Ibbhas..."
“They do not honor brahmins, they do not revere brahmins, they do not esteem brahmins,
they do not worship brahmins, they do not pay respect to brahmins. In this way,
the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha uttered this first slur against the Sakyan clan.
2.2. The Second Claim of Inferiority “But what, Ambaṭṭha, have the Sakyans done against you?
“Once, Master Gotama, on a certain occasion, I went to Kapilavatthu on some business for my teacher, the brahmin Pokkharasāti.”
I went to where the assembly hall of the Sakyans was.
Now at that time, many Sakyans and Sakyan youths were seated on high seats in the assembly hall,
laughing and playing with one another by poking each other with their fingers, doing nothing else but mocking me alone.
"I suspect they are mocking me; no one even invited me to a seat.

This, Master Gotama, is improper; this is unbecoming, that these Sakyans, being of ignoble stock and being indeed ignoble, do not honor brahmins, do not revere brahmins, do not esteem brahmins, and do not..."
“They honor brahmins; they do not show respect to brahmins.
Thus did the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha utter this second slur against the Sakyan outcasts.
2.3. The Third Slur Against the Outcasts (Tatiya-ibbhavāda)
“Even a little quail, Ambaṭṭha, cackles lustfully only in its own nest.
And this, Ambaṭṭha, is the Sakyans’ own [nest], namely Kapilavatthu; it is not fitting for the venerable Ambaṭṭha to be angry over such a trifle.
“There are these four castes, Master Gotama:”
Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas.
For among these four castes, Master Gotama, there are three castes—
the khattiyas, the vessas, and the suddas— [who live by various crafts].
On the contrary, they have merely become attendants to the brahmins.
Sir Gotama, this is not fitting, this is not proper, that these Sakyas, being of ignoble stock and remaining so,
do not honor the brahmins, do not revere the brahmins, and do not respect the brahmins.
“They honor brahmins, they do not show respect to brahmins.
Thus did the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha level this third charge of outcaste status against the Sakyans.
2.4. The Charge of Being the Son of a Slave Girl.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"This young man Ambaṭṭha insults the Sakyans excessively by calling them 'outcasts. What if I were to ask him about his clan?
Then the Blessed One said this to the young man Ambaṭṭha:
“What is your clan, Ambaṭṭha?
“I am a Kaṇhāyana, Master Gotama.
“But, Ambaṭṭha, when you recollect your ancient maternal and paternal lineage, the Sakyans are the sons of noble fathers; you are the son of a slave-girl to the Sakyans.”
Moreover, Ambaṭṭha, the Sakyans regard King Okkāka as their grandfather.
Once upon a time, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka, wishing to transfer the kingdom to the son of his chief queen—who was beloved and dear to him—banished his eldest sons from the realm:
Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍa, Hatthinika, and Sinisūra.
Banished from that kingdom, they settled on the slopes of the Himalayas by the shore of a lotus pond where there was a great thicket of *sāka* plants; there they made their dwelling.
Out of fear of the loss of their caste, they entered into sexual relations with their own sisters.
Then, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka addressed his ministers and counselors:
“Where, sir, are the princes living now?
“There is, Your Majesty, a large grove of sāla trees on the bank of a lotus pond at the foot of the Himalayas; there the princes are living now.
Out of fear of the destruction of their lineage, they are having sexual intercourse with their own sisters.”
Then, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Truly, these princes are Sakyans! Truly, these princes are supreme Sakyans!
It was from that time on, Ambaṭṭha, that they became known as the Sakyans, and he was their forefather.
Now, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka had a slave girl named Disā.
She gave birth to a son named Kaṇha.
As soon as he was born, Kaṇha spoke:
“‘Wash me, mother! Bathe me, mother! Deliver me from this impurity; I shall be for your welfare!
Now, Ambaṭṭha, just as people nowadays perceive piśācas when they see them and recognize them as ‘piśācas,’ even so, Ambaṭṭha, at that time people perceived piśācas and recognized them as ‘Kaṇhas.’”
They said this:
“This one, when born, spoke; a Kanhāyana has been born, a Piśāca has been born.
And from that time on, Ambaṭṭha, they are known as the Kanhāyanas, and he was the original ancestor of the Kanhāyanas.
"Thus indeed, Ambaṭṭha, as you recollect your ancient maternal and paternal lineage and family name, the Sakyans are the sons of noble men, while you are the son of a slave-girl of the Sakyans.
When this was said, those young brahmins said to the Blessed One:
"May Master Gotama not excessively insult Ambaṭṭha with the term 'son of a slave-girl'."
"Master Gotama, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is well-born; the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is of good family;
the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is learned; the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is eloquent; the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is wise;
and the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is capable of conversing with Master Gotama on this matter."
Then the Blessed One said this to those young brahmins:
"If it occurs to you, young brahmins, thus:
'Ambaṭṭha the young brahmin is ill-born; Ambaṭṭha the young brahmin is not of good family; Ambaṭṭha the young brahmin has little learning...'"
“The young man Ambaṭṭha has poor speech; the young man Ambaṭṭha is witless;
the young man Ambaṭṭha is not capable of conversing with the ascetic Gotama on this matter.
Let the young man Ambaṭṭha be; you yourselves may converse with me on this matter.
But if it occurs to you young men thus:
‘Ambaṭṭha the young man is well-born, Ambaṭṭha the young man is of good family, Ambaṭṭha the young man is learned,
Ambaṭṭha the young man is eloquent, Ambaṭṭha the young man is wise, and Ambaṭṭha the young man is capable’— then [you should know this].
“Let the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha debate this matter with the ascetic Gotama; you all stay back.
Let the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha debate with me.
“Master Gotama, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is well-born, he is a man of noble family, and he is highly learned.”
“The young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is eloquent; the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is well-spoken; the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is wise;
and the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is capable of conversing with Master Gotama on this matter. We shall remain silent;
let the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha converse with Master Gotama on this matter.”
Then the Blessed One said this to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha:
“Ambaṭṭha, this question, moreover, comes to you in accordance with the Dhamma; it must be answered even against your will.
If you do not answer it, or if you evade it with something else, or if you remain silent, or if you depart, right here your head shall split into seven pieces.”

"What do you think, Ambaṭṭha, what have you heard from the aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking: from where did the Kaṇhāyanas originate, and who was the ancestor of the Kaṇhāyanas?
When this was said, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha remained silent.
A second time, the Blessed One said this to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha:

“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha? What have you heard from the aged, elderly, and venerable brahmins—the teachers of teachers—when they were speaking: from what origin did the Kaṇhāyanas come, and who was the ancestor of the Kaṇhāyanas?
A second time, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha remained silent.
Then the Blessed One said this to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha:
“Answer now, Ambaṭṭha; this is no longer the time for silence.
For, Ambaṭṭha, if one does not answer a question put by the Tathāgata in accordance with the Dhamma up to the third time, his head shall split into seven pieces right there.”
Now at that time, the yakkha Vajirapāṇī, taking a great iron club—blazing, flaming, and glowing—stood in the air above the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, thinking:
"If this young brahmin Ambaṭṭha does not answer a legitimate question posed by the Blessed One up to a third time, I shall split his head into seven pieces right here.
The Blessed One saw that yakkha Vajirapāṇī, and the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha saw him as well.

Then the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, terrified, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, seeking refuge in the Blessed One alone, seeking shelter in the Blessed One alone, and seeking protection in the Blessed One alone, sat down near him and said this to the Blessed One:
"What did Master Gotama say?
Let Master Gotama speak again."
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha, what have you heard from the elder,
mature brahmins— the teachers of teachers— when they were speaking, as to where the Kaṇhāyanas originated and who was the ancestor of the Kaṇhāyanas?
“Just so, Master Gotama, have I heard it, exactly as Master Gotama has said.”
“From him descended the Upabhūtikas Kaṇhāyanas;
he was the original ancestor of the Kaṇhāyanas.
2.5. The Discourse on the Ambaṭṭha Lineage.
When this was said, those young brahmins became noisy, raising a loud clamor and a great din:
"Ambaṭṭha the young brahmin is indeed ill-born, sirs! Ambaṭṭha the young brahmin is indeed not of a good family, sirs!
Ambaṭṭha the young brahmin is indeed the son of a slave-girl among the Sakyans, sirs! The Sakyans are indeed the sons of Ambaṭṭha the young brahmin’s master, sirs!"
“We have surely thought that we should disparage the ascetic Gotama, who speaks only the truth.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“These young men are excessively insulting the young man Ambaṭṭha by calling him the son of a slave-girl; what if I were to set him free?”
Then the Blessed One said this to those young brahmins:
"Young brahmins, do not revile the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha excessively with the term 'son of a slave-girl.
That Kaṇha was a sublime seer."
So, having gone to the southern country and mastered the Brahma-mantras, he approached King Okkāka and asked for his daughter Maddarūpī.
At this, King Okkāka, thinking, "Who is this?
How can he, being the son of a slave-girl, ask for my daughter Maddarūpī?", became angry and displeased, and fixed an arrow to his bow.
Thus, young men, the minister was unable both to release that arrow nor to withdraw it.
Then the ministers and courtiers approached the seer Kaṇha and said this:
“May it be well with the king, venerable sir!”
“May it be well with the king, venerable sir.
“It will be well with the king; however, if the king releases his arrow even slightly downward, the earth as far as the king’s realm extends will be shaken.
“May it be well with the king, venerable sir; may it be well with the country.”

“‘There will be safety for the king, there will be safety for the country; however, if the king releases his arrow upwards, for as long as it takes to traverse the king’s realm, the rain-god will not send rain for seven years.
‘May there be safety, venerable sir! May there be safety for the king and the country, and may the rain-god send rain!

‘There will be safety for the king, there will be safety for the country, and the rain-god will send rain; however, let the king fix his arrow upon his eldest son, and the prince will remain safe and unharmed.’”
Then, young men, the ministers informed Okkāka:
"Let Okkāka fix his arrow upon the eldest prince; thus the prince will be safe and sound.
Thereupon King Okkāka fixed his arrow upon the eldest prince, and the prince became safe and sound.

Then King Okkāka, terrified, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, being struck by the Brahma-punishment, gave him his daughter Maddarūpī. "Do not, young men, excessively insult the young man Ambaṭṭha with the term 'son of a slave-girl'; that Kaṇha was a sublime seer. 3. The Preeminence of the Kṣatriya [The Buddha continued: "In this way, Ambaṭṭha, the lineage of the Kṣatriyas is the most excellent among human lineages. For what reason? Because, Ambaṭṭha, the Kṣatriya is the one who is consecrated by sprinkling water (abhisitta-muddhāvasitta). And how, Ambaṭṭha, is a Kṣatriya consecrated by sprinkling water? Here, Ambaṭṭha, they prepare a high throne for the Kṣatriya, and they bring forward a white bull, a white cow, a white goat, a white ram, and a white cock; they also bring forward a golden vessel filled with water from a great lake.

Then, Ambaṭṭha, the royal chaplain, together with the Purohita’s sons, the Brahmin youths, and the courtiers, sprinkles the head of the Kṣatriya with water from the golden vessel. This, Ambaṭṭha, is how a Kṣatriya is consecrated by sprinkling water. It is because of this, Ambaṭṭha, that the Kṣatriya is the most excellent among human lineages. Then the Blessed One addressed the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha:
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
Suppose here a kṣatriya youth were to have sexual intercourse with a brahmin girl, and as a result of that union a son were born to them.”
“If a son is born to a kshatriya youth by a brahmin girl, would he receive a seat or water among the brahmins?
“He would, Master Gotama.
“Would the brahmins feed him at a funeral sacrifice, at a rice-porridge offering, at a sacrificial rite, or at a guest-meal?”
“They would feed him, Master Gotama.
“Would the brahmins teach him the mantras or not?
“They would teach him them, Master Gotama.”
“Would he have any sense of shame regarding women, whether they were veiled or unveiled?
“He would have no sense of shame regarding them, Master Gotama.
“Would the kṣatriyas then anoint him with the kṣatriya consecration?”
“No, Master Gotama.
“For what reason?
“Because, Master Gotama, it is not possible from the mother’s side.”
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
Suppose here a brahmin youth were to have sexual intercourse with a kṣatriya maiden, and from that union a son were born.
Would that son, born of a brahmin youth and a kṣatriya maiden, receive a seat or water among the brahmins?”
“He would, Master Gotama.
“Would the brahmins then feed him at a funeral feast, or at a rice-offering, or at a sacrifice, or at a guest-meal?
“They would, Master Gotama.”
“Would the brahmins teach him the mantras or not?
“They would, Master Gotama.
“Would he have any restrictions regarding women or none?”
“Because it would be uncovered, Master Gotama.
“Would the kṣatriyas then consecrate him with the kṣatriya consecration?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, Master Gotama, he was not born from his father.
“Thus, Ambaṭṭha, whether by making a woman out of a woman or a man out of a man, the Khattiyas alone are the best; the Brahmins are inferior.”
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
Suppose here the brahmins, on account of some offense, were to shave a brahmin bald, beat him with a bundle of straw, and banish him from the kingdom or the city.
Would he receive a seat or water among the brahmins?”
“No, Master Gotama.
“Would the brahmins then feed him at a funeral feast, or at a meal of rice-porridge, or at a sacrifice, or at a guest-meal?
“No, Master Gotama.”
“Would the brahmins teach him the mantras, or not?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“Would he have access to women, or would he not?”
“Because it would be a source of reproach for him, Master Gotama.
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
Suppose here some kṣatriyas, on account of some offense, were to shave a fellow kṣatriya’s head with a razor, strike him with a bag of ashes, and banish him from the kingdom or the city.”
“Would he receive a seat or water among the brahmins?
“He would, Master Gotama.
“And would the brahmins feed him at a funeral feast, or at a rice-offering, or at a sacrifice, or at a guest-meal?”
“They would feed him, Master Gotama.
“Would the brahmins teach him the mantras or not?
“They would teach him, Master Gotama.”
“Is he, moreover, shut out from women or not?
“He is not shut out from them, Master Gotama.
“In this respect, Ambaṭṭha, a kshatriya has reached the ultimate degradation when the kshatriyas have him shaved with a razor, beaten with a staff, and banished from the kingdom or the city.”
Thus, Ambaṭṭha, even when a khattiya has reached the lowest state, the khattiyas are still superior and the brahmins inferior.
Ambaṭṭha, this verse was spoken by Brahmā Sanankumāra:
“The khattiya is the best among people...”
Those who rely on their clan;
but one endowed with true knowledge and conduct is the best among gods and humans.”
Moreover, Ambaṭṭha, this verse was well-sung, not ill-sung, well-spoken, not ill-spoken, meaningful, not meaningless, by Brahmā Sanankumāra; it was approved by me as well.
For I too, Ambaṭṭha, say thus:
"The khattiya is the best among people..."
Those who rely on their clan;
but one endowed with true knowledge and conduct is the best among gods and humans.”
The first section for recitation.
4. The Discourse on True Knowledge and Conduct:
“But what, Master Gotama, is that conduct, and what is that true knowledge?”
“Indeed, Ambaṭṭha, in the possession of supreme true knowledge and conduct, there is no talk of birth, no talk of clan, nor talk of pride such as:
‘Are you worthy of me, or are you not worthy of me?

But where, Ambaṭṭha, there is giving in marriage or taking in marriage, or both giving and taking in marriage—it is there that this talk of birth, this talk of clan, and this talk of pride are found.”
‘Are you worthy of me, or are you not worthy of me?

Ambaṭṭha, whoever is bound by talk of birth, or bound by talk of clan, or bound by talk of pride, or bound by talk of marriage alliances, they are far from the unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct.

Having abandoned, Ambaṭṭha, being bound by talk of birth, being bound by talk of clan, being bound by talk of pride, and being bound by talk of marriage alliances, there is the realization of the unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct.”
“But what, Master Gotama, is that conduct, and what is that true knowledge?

“Here, Ambaṭṭha, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.”
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Endowed with that acquisition of faith, he reflects thus:

“… [omitted] … He, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
… [omitted] … This too is part of his conduct.”
Furthermore, Ambaṭṭha, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,

a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This, too, is part of his conduct.
Furthermore, Ambaṭṭha, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He is equanimous, mindful, and abides in happiness. ...pe...
This too belongs to his conduct.
Furthermore, Ambaṭṭha, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity …pe…
This too belongs to his conduct.
This, Ambaṭṭha, is that conduct.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward knowledge and vision. …pe…
This too is his true knowledge:
“… he understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being’;
this too is his true knowledge.”
This, Ambaṭṭha, is that true knowledge.
This, Ambaṭṭha, is called a bhikkhu who is “accomplished in true knowledge,” “accomplished in conduct,” and “accomplished in both true knowledge and conduct.
And, Ambaṭṭha, there is no other accomplishment in true knowledge or accomplishment in conduct higher or more sublime than this accomplishment in true knowledge and this accomplishment in conduct.
5. The Four Gateways to Decline.
Ambaṭṭha, through this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct, there are four gateways to decline.
What are the four?

"In this case, Ambaṭṭha, a certain ascetic or brahmin, failing to attain this very unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct, takes up a carrying-pole and plunges into a forest region, thinking:
'I shall subsist on fallen fruit.
But he turns out to be nothing other than an attendant to one who is truly endowed with true knowledge and conduct."
Ambaṭṭha, this is the first door to ruin for one who fails to achieve this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct.
Furthermore, Ambaṭṭha, here some ascetic or brahmin,
failing to achieve this very unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct and failing to subsist on fallen fruit, takes up a spade and a basket.
He plunges deep into the forest wilderness with the thought, "I shall subsist on bulbs, roots, and fruits. Yet, in reality,
he ends up becoming merely an attendant to one who is perfected in both knowledge and conduct.
Ambaṭṭha, this is the second door to the state of deprivation resulting from this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct.
Furthermore, Ambaṭṭha, here some ascetic or brahmin, being unable to achieve this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct,
and being unable to subsist on fallen fruit, [resorts to] subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits.
Failing to achieve this, he builds a fire-sanctuary near a village or near a town and dwells there tending the fire;
yet he turns out to be nothing more than an attendant to one who is truly endowed with true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*).
Ambaṭṭha, this is the third door to the state of loss resulting from this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct.
Furthermore, Ambaṭṭha, here some ascetic or brahmin, being unable to achieve this unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct,
being unable to subsist on fallen fruit, being unable to subsist on roots and fruits,
and being unable to tend the sacred fire, [sets up] a four-doored shelter at a crossroads.
Having built a house, he dwells there thinking:
“Whatever ascetic or brahmin comes from these four directions, I shall honor them according to my ability and according to my strength.
Yet, in fact, he becomes merely an attendant to one who is truly endowed with true knowledge and conduct.
Ambaṭṭha, this is the fourth gateway to ruin for this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct.
Ambaṭṭha, these are the four gateways to ruin for this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct.
What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
“Do you, along with your teacher, manifest this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct?
“No indeed, Master Gotama.
Who am I, Master Gotama, to have a teacher? And what is this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct?”
“I am far removed, Master Gotama, from the supreme perfection of true knowledge and conduct, along with my teachers.
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
Since you have not attained this very supreme perfection of true knowledge and conduct, did you go deep into the forest wilderness along with your teachers, taking up a carrying-pole?”
‘I shall subsist on windfall fruit,’ would you do so?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?”

“Did you, failing to attain this very supreme perfection of knowledge and conduct, and failing to subsist on windfallen fruit, enter the depths of the forest and jungle with your teacher, taking up spade and basket, thinking:
‘We shall subsist on bulbs, roots, and fruits’?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
Since you are unable to attain this unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct, and since you are unable to subsist on windfallen fruit,
and since you are unable to subsist on roots and fruits, would you not rather [live] near a village?”
“Or have you, Ambaṭṭha, together with your teacher, stayed here having built a fire-sanctuary at the edge of a village and tending the sacred fire?
“No indeed, Master Gotama.
“What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?”
"Is it because you are unable to attain this very supreme perfection of true knowledge and conduct,
and unable to subsist on fallen fruit, unable to subsist on roots and fruits, and unable to maintain the fire-sacrifice,
that you, together with your teacher, have built a house with four doors at a crossroads and dwell there?"
“‘Whatever ascetic or brahmin comes from these four directions, we shall honor him according to our ability and according to our strength,’ is that not so?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“In this way, Ambaṭṭha, you and your teacher have fallen away from this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct.”

And these four doors to the states of deprivation exist for one who has failed to attain the unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct; from these you have fallen away, along with your teacher.
Furthermore, Ambaṭṭha, this speech was uttered by your own teacher, the brahmin Pokkharasāti:

“Who are those shaveling ascetics, those outcasts, those dark fellows, the descendants of our kinsman’s heels? What conversation can there be between them and the brahmins learned in the three Vedas?”—he who himself was deficient and lacked the qualities leading to the higher realms.
See, Ambaṭṭha, how far you have failed your teacher, the brahmin Pokkharasāti!

For the brahmin Pokkharasāti, Ambaṭṭha, eats the food provided by King Pasenadi of Kosala. 6. Inquiry into the State of Being an Ancient Seer Furthermore, Ambaṭṭha, the brahmin Pokkharasāti eats the food given by King Pasenadi of Kosala.
King Pasenadi of Kosala would not even grant him an audience.
Even when he consulted with him, he did so through a curtain.
Now, Ambaṭṭha, if one were to accept the lawful alms-offering presented by him, how could King Pasenadi of Kosala not grant him an audience?
See, Ambaṭṭha, how far you have erred against your teacher, the brahmin Pokkharasāti.
What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?

Suppose here King Pasenadi of Kosala, seated on the neck of an elephant, or seated on the back of a horse, or standing on the floor of a chariot, were to deliberate upon some matter with the uggas or the rājaññas.
So, having departed from that place, he would stand to one side.
Then a slave or a slave’s son might come and, standing in that very place, recite that same counsel, saying:
“Thus spoke King Pasenadi of Kosala; thus spoke King Pasenadi of Kosala.”
“Would he speak what was spoken by the king, or deliberate on the king’s counsel?
To that extent would he be a king or one who considers himself a king?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“In the same way, Ambaṭṭha, you [should know] those ancient brahmin seers who were the makers of the mantras,
the promulgators of the mantras— those whose ancient mantra-words, sung, promulgated, and compiled, the brahmins of today sing along,
repeat after, recite what was spoken, and teach what was taught; namely, Aṭṭhaka...”

‘I study these mantras along with my teacher: Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu’—by that much alone, Ambaṭṭha, it is impossible for you to be a seer or one practicing for the state of a seer.
What do you think about this?
What have you heard from the elder and venerable brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking—
those ancient seers who were the makers of the mantras and the promulgators of the mantras,
whose ancient mantra-words, chanted, proclaimed, and compiled, the brahmins of today still sing along with and recite?
They repeat what has been spoken and recite what has been chanted, namely: Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu.
Thus they are well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beards trimmed, adorned with jeweled earrings and ornaments, and dressed in white garments.
“Are they provided with and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure and divert themselves, just as you and your teacher do now?
“No, Master Gotama. [The Buddha continued:
“Do they eat rice cooked with fine meat broth, from which the black grains have been picked out, served with many soups and many curries, just as you and your teacher do now?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“… [as before] …”
“Do they indeed amuse themselves with women whose limbs are bound by golden bands, just as you do now together with your teacher?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“… [as before] …”
“Is it not so that they, with their horses’ tails as whips and long goads, pierce their mounts as they drive them about, just as you and your teacher do now?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“… [as before] …”
“Is it thus that they have you guarded by men with long swords in cities where the moats are dug deep and the crossbars are lowered—just as you and your teacher are now?
“No, indeed, Master Gotama.
“In that case, Ambaṭṭha, neither you nor your teacher are a seer, nor do you practice for the sake of being a seer.”
"But, Ambaṭṭha, whoever has doubt or uncertainty regarding me, let him question me; I shall clear it up for him with an explanation.
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from his dwelling, stood up on the walking-path.
The young brahmin Ambaṭṭha also emerged from his dwelling and set out upon the walking-path.
Then, as the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha walked back and forth following the Blessed One who was walking, he examined the Blessed One’s body for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The young brahmin Ambaṭṭha saw the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Blessed One’s body, with the exception of two.
He wavered, was perplexed, was not convinced, and did not have faith regarding two of the marks of a Great Man:
the sheathed organ and the long tongue.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
“This young man Ambaṭṭha has indeed seen in me, with few exceptions, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
He wavers, doubts, is not convinced, and does not have faith regarding two of the marks of a Great Man:
the sheathed genitals and the large tongue.”
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha saw the Blessed One’s private parts withdrawn within a sheath.
Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue, licked both ear-holes and rubbed them; he licked both nostrils and rubbed them; and he covered the entire circle of his forehead with his tongue.
Then this thought occurred to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha:
“The ascetic Gotama is indeed endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, complete and not incomplete.
Then he said this to the Blessed One:
“Now, Master Gotama, let us depart; we have many duties and much to do.”
“Now, Ambaṭṭha, you may go at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Then the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha mounted a chariot drawn by mares and departed.
At that time, the brahmin Pokkharasāti had come out from Ukkaṭṭhā and was sitting in his own park together with a large company of brahmins, waiting for the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha.
Then the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha set out for his own monastery.
Having gone by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle, he alighted from the carriage and approached the brahmin Pokkharasāti on foot.
Having approached, he paid homage to the brahmin Pokkharasāti and sat down to one side.
When the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha was seated to one side, the brahmin Pokkharasāti said this to him:
"Dear Ambaṭṭha, did you see that venerable Gotama?
"We saw that venerable Gotama, sir," he replied.
“Is it true, dear Ambaṭṭha, that the report concerning the venerable Gotama has arisen exactly as he is, and not otherwise?
Is the venerable Gotama indeed such as that report describes, and not otherwise?
“It is exactly as he is, sir, that the report concerning the venerable Gotama has arisen, and not otherwise. The venerable Gotama is indeed such as that report describes, and not otherwise.”
“Moreover, that venerable Gotama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, complete and not incomplete.
“But did you, dear Ambaṭṭha, have any conversation or discussion with the ascetic Gotama?
“I did, sir; I had some conversation and discussion with the ascetic Gotama.”
“But how was it, dear Ambaṭṭha, that you had some conversation with the ascetic Gotama?
Then the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha reported to the brahmin Pokkharasāti everything that had been the entire conversation with the Blessed One.
When this was said, the brahmin Pokkharasāti said this to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha:
“Alas for us, you pseudo-wise one! Alas for us, you pseudo-learned one! Alas for us, you pseudo-triple-knowledge holder!
For it seems that a man such as this, a benefactor to us, upon the breakup of the body, after death, would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell!”
Ambaṭṭha, because you spoke thus, repeatedly insulting the venerable Gotama, he too spoke to us, repeatedly leading us on:

"Oh, what a 'wise man' we have here! Oh, what a 'learned man' we have here! Oh, what a 'master of the three Vedas' we have here! Indeed, sir, a man such as this, acting for his own interest, will—upon the breakup of the body, after death—fall into a state of deprivation."
“...might he be reborn in a state of misery, a fallen state, or in hell,” being thus provoked and displeased, he sent the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha away on foot.
And at that very moment, he desired to approach the Blessed One for an audience.
8. Pokkharasāti’s Visit to the Buddha
Then those brahmins said this to the brahmin Pokkharasāti:
“It is far too late today, sir, to approach the ascetic Gotama for an audience.
Let the venerable Pokkharasāti approach the ascetic Gotama for an audience tomorrow.”
Then the brahmin Pokkharasāti had exquisite hard and soft food prepared in his own residence;
having loaded it onto vehicles, he set out from Ukkaṭṭhā with torches being carried before him, heading toward the forest grove of Icchānaṅgala.
Having traveled by vehicle as far as the ground would permit, he alighted from the vehicle and approached the Blessed One on foot.
Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One; and when they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the brahmin Pokkharasāti said this to the Blessed One:
"Has our pupil, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, come here, Master Gotama?"
“Your pupil, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, has indeed come to you, brahmin.
“But did you, Master Gotama, have any conversation or exchange of words with the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha?
“I did, brahmin, I had some conversation and exchange of words with the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha.”
“But how, Master Gotama, did your conversation with the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha proceed?
Then the Blessed One related to the brahmin Pokkharasāti the entire course of his conversation with the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha.
When this was said, the brahmin Pokkharasāti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Master Gotama, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is a fool; may Master Gotama forgive the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha.
“May the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha be happy, brahmin,” [the Blessed One replied].
Then the brahmin Pokkharasāti examined the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Blessed One’s body.
The brahmin Pokkharasāti saw on the Blessed One’s body thirty-two of the marks of a Great Man, with the exception of two.
Regarding two of these marks of a Great Man— he was doubtful, perplexed, undecided,
and lacked confidence concerning the sheathed genitals and the large tongue.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"This brahmin Pokkharasāti sees my thirty-two marks of a Great Man, with the exception of two.
Regarding two of the marks of a Great Man, he is perplexed, doubtful, undecided, and lacks confidence."
"And his private parts are enclosed in a sheath, and he has a long tongue.
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernormal power that the brahmin Pokkharasāti saw the Blessed One’s private parts enclosed in a sheath.
Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue, licked and touched both ear-holes; he licked and touched both nostrils; and he covered the entire circle of his forehead with his tongue.
Then it occurred to the brahmin Pokkharasāti:
"The ascetic Gotama is indeed endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, complete and not incomplete.
He said this to the Blessed One:
“May the venerable Gotama accept today’s meal from me, together with the community of monks.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the brahmin Pokkharasāti, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, announced that it was time for the Blessed One.
“It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, approached the residence of the brahmin Pokkharasāti together with the community of monks. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.

Then the brahmin Pokkharasāti, with his own hands, personally served and satisfied the Blessed One with excellent hard and soft foods, and the young brahmin students likewise served the community of monks.
Then the brahmin Pokkharasāti, when the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, took a low seat and sat down to one side.
As the brahmin Pokkharasāti was sitting there, the Blessed One gave him a graduated discourse, namely:
talk on giving, talk on virtue, and talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.

When the Blessed One knew that the brahmin Pokkharasāti was ready in heart, pliant in heart, free from hindrances in heart, uplifted in heart, and serene in heart, he then set forth that Dhamma exposition which is uniquely realized by Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take up the dye;
In the same way, even as he sat there, the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye arose in the brahmin Pokkharasāti:
"Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.
9. Pokkharasāti’s Declaration of Lay Followership.
Then the brahmin Pokkharasāti, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma;

having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, and having attained self-confidence through fearlessness in the Teacher’s instruction, being independent of others, said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!”
"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden,
or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Gotama in many ways."
"Venerable Gotama, I, together with my sons, my wife, my retinue, and my ministers, go for refuge to the Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Venerable Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
And just as the Venerable Gotama visits other lay families in Ukkaṭṭhā, may the Venerable Gotama likewise visit the family of Pokkharasāti."
"In that regard, those young men or young women who will pay homage to Master Gotama,
or rise up for him, or offer him a seat or water, or whose minds will find confidence— this will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
"It is well said, brahmin," [the Blessed One replied].
The Ambaṭṭha Sutta is finished; the third.
